item.title: Standard Chartered: Gold must hold $3,886 or risk deeper correction as oil fuels hike bets
item.description:
Oil is the key driver here: Standard Chartered’s warning ties gold’s next move directly to crude, with each leg higher in oil feeding inflation and Fed hike expectations, a pressure gold has struggled to withstand. With a December hike largely priced, any hawkish tone from the Fed on Wednesday could push gold toward the $3,886 support. A break there could trigger further liquidation from underwater ETP holders. On the other side, positioning is at its lightest since May and short covering has started, which leaves room for a sharp rebound if oil eases or the dollar softens. Physical buying around Diwali is a near-term test of whether Asian demand can step in where Western investors have pulled back.

-

Standard Chartered still sees gold higher by early next year, but says it first needs to find a floor while rising oil keeps the Fed in hiking mode.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered says gold must hold $3,886 support after falling below $4,000, warning that a sustained break could bring a much deeper correction.
  • Higher oil prices are keeping inflation risks and Fed tightening expectations in focus. Markets price under a 10% chance of a hike this week and around 86% odds in December.
  • The 10-year Treasury yield has eased to just under 5%, but this has given gold little support, and the dollar remains a major headwind.
  • Gold ETPs saw renewed outflows late last week, and at least 350 tonnes of ETP holdings are now in loss-making territory. Speculative positioning is at its lowest since May after eight weeks of cuts.
  • Indian imports fell 83% in September, but Diwali on November 8 could revive buying. Chinese imports rose 34% to around 145 tonnes.
  • The bank kept its forecasts for gold to average $4,650 in Q4 and $4,850 in Q1 2027.

Gold needs to establish a floor after slipping below $4,000 an ounce, or risks a much deeper correction, Standard Chartered warned, with higher oil prices keeping inflation risks and further Federal Reserve tightening in focus, according to the bank’s latest precious metals report as reported by Kitco.

Suki Cooper, Standard Chartered’s global head of commodities research, said gold needs to hold support at $3,886. A sustained break below that level could expose the market to a significantly larger decline, even though a two-month downtrend has pushed prices close to oversold territory. Cooper said elevated energy prices continue to push inflation pressure higher, forcing investors to reassess the outlook for US monetary policy and weighing on the metal.

Standard Chartered said markets see less than a 10% chance of a Fed rate hike at Wednesday’s meeting but price around 86% odds of a move in December, after the US midterm elections. The 10-year Treasury yield has eased to just under 5% from around 5.3% earlier this month, but Cooper said the drop has done little for gold, with investors focused on persistent inflation and the risk of more tightening. The US dollar remains a major headwind, with gold’s three-month rolling correlation with the greenback at minus 47%.

Investment demand has softened. Global gold-backed exchange-traded products, or ETPs, saw renewed outflows late last week, with holdings down 1.3 tonnes, although October flows remain marginally positive. Cooper said the sell-off extended across asset classes, reflecting technology-sector jitters and investors raising cash to meet margin calls. She estimated that at least 350 tonnes of ETP holdings are now in loss-making territory at current prices, which could leave the market vulnerable to further liquidation.

Positioning, however, may be nearing a turning point. Speculative investors have cut their gold exposure for eight straight weeks, taking positioning to its lowest level since May, and Cooper said some short covering suggests speculators may be starting to look for a floor.

Asian physical demand could also offer support. Indian imports fell 83% year on year in September to around 14 tonnes, the weakest monthly level since January 2023, as a weak monsoon and high prices delayed seasonal buying. Cooper said demand could pick up ahead of the Diwali festival on November 8 as retailers restock. Chinese imports rose 34% to around 145 tonnes in September, taking the year-to-date total to around 1,290 tonnes, up 67%.

Despite the near-term risks, the bank kept its forecasts for gold to average $4,650 in the fourth quarter and $4,850 in the first quarter of 2027, noting that central banks and ETP investors have generally treated price corrections as buying opportunities this year. Cooper cautioned that the coming weeks could stay volatile, with gold likely to keep testing its floor if oil prices extend their gains and keep inflation expectations elevated.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman: Markets selling US banks on higher rates, but income guidance rises into 2027
item.description:
Goldman’s view puts bank stocks at the centre of the debate over higher-for-longer rates: with the Fed still on a hiking path, unrealised bond losses are keeping investors away despite improving income guidance. If yields stabilise, or the regulatory changes Goldman flags make 2027 buybacks more likely, the gap between earnings and share prices could narrow quickly. Deposits pooling in the largest lenders point to more pressure on regional and smaller bank funding costs. The credit team’s preference for secured, collateral-backed lending over unsecured bonds is a cautious signal for the heavy pipeline of AI-related bond supply.

---

Earlier:

  • ICYMI: S&P sees global bond issuance growth slowing to 2.7% in 2027, weakest in five years

---

Goldman says US banks are being sold for what higher rates do to their bond portfolios, not for what those rates are doing to their earnings, and it thinks the gap is the opportunity.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs says around 80% of early-reporting S&P 500 companies beat Q3 earnings estimates, but market reactions have been muted as higher yields shift the focus to margin durability, earnings quality and 2027 guidance.
  • US banks reported robust fundamentals: net interest income guidance extended into 2027, equity trading surged and credit metrics stayed benign.
  • Bank shares still fell. Goldman says investors are focused on capital pressure from unrealised bond losses, which it sees as largely a timing issue, with regulatory changes possibly supporting buybacks in 2027.
  • Several bank CEOs flagged a once-in-a-generation capital shortage to fund the AI boom, while rejecting third-party agentic AI transacting on client accounts on security grounds.
  • Goldman’s credit team prefers secured, amortising loans against collateral and contracts over unsecured bonds.
  • The top 10 US banks captured around 85% of Q3 deposit growth, with one bank taking around 30%. Consumer activity and credit trends remain broadly healthy.

Goldman Sachs says US bank shares have been punished despite strong third-quarter results, arguing that investors are trading on a single idea, that higher rates mean selling financials, while overlooking guidance for rising interest income into 2027, according to a third-quarter earnings review from the firm.

Corporate results have been resilient overall. Goldman said roughly 80% of the early-reporting S&P 500 companies beat earnings estimates, but equity market reactions to those beats have been muted. With investors weighing the impact of higher yields, the focus has moved away from headline quarterly beats toward how durable margins are, the quality of earnings and whether forward guidance through 2027 is credible.

Banks, typically among the first to report, delivered solid numbers. Goldman said guidance for net interest income, the gap between what banks earn on loans and securities and what they pay on deposits, was extended into 2027 as fixed-rate assets reprice at higher yields. Equity trading revenue surged and credit metrics remained benign.

The bank argues that the market’s response reflects the two-sided effect of higher rates. Rising rates lift interest income but also weigh on capital through unrealised losses on bond portfolios, and Goldman believes that capital side is where investor attention is concentrated. It sees the gap between those two effects as the potential opportunity, describing capital pressure as largely a matter of timing and noting that upcoming regulatory changes could support share buybacks in 2027. Most banks that provided guidance expect interest income and net interest margins to keep rising into 2027.

AI featured prominently in bank commentary. Several chief executives warned of a once-in-a-generation capital shortage to fund the AI boom, while also rejecting third-party agentic AI, meaning autonomous software agents, carrying out transactions on client accounts because of security concerns, even as their own internal AI tools scaled rapidly. Goldman’s credit team sees a similar divide in AI more broadly, with demand intact but access to funding now separating winners from the rest. The team remains cautious, favouring secured, amortising loans backed by collateral and contracts over unsecured bonds.

Concentration in the sector is also rising. Goldman said the 10 largest US banks captured roughly 85% of third-quarter deposit growth, and a single bank took around 30%, leaving little for the more than 4,200 remaining institutions.

On consumers, Goldman’s consumer sector analyst Cecile Origenes said pressure at lower income levels has not translated into broad deterioration, and that the more important question as earnings season continues is where consumers are still prepared to spend and which companies can capture that demand without sacrificing margins. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: S&P sees global bond issuance growth slowing to 2.7% in 2027, weakest in five years
item.description:
A sharp slowdown in supply growth would ease one source of pressure on bond markets after a heavy 2026, which could help keep corporate spreads tight if demand holds up. AI borrowing stays the main swing factor for supply: with capex expected to top $1.3 trillion, hyperscaler issuance will keep testing investor appetite for technology credit. The reference to the Middle East war links the outlook to oil. Any renewed rise in crude would feed inflation, push back hopes of lower rates and strengthen the headwinds S&P describes. A growing share of Chinese debt in global benchmarks would also gradually leave index-tracking funds more exposed to Chinese rate moves.

---

Earlier:

  • ICYMI: Fitch sees Fed hiking to 4.25% in December, says US credit outlook still benign

---

After a bumper 2026, S&P expects growth in global bond issuance to slow to a crawl next year, though AI borrowing and refinancing needs mean the debt keeps coming.

Summary:

  • S&P Global Ratings forecasts global bond issuance growth of 2.7% in 2027, down from an estimated 12.2% in 2026 and the slowest pace in five years.
  • Total global issuance is expected to reach around $11.7 trillion this year.
  • Higher interest rates and uncertainty linked to the Middle East war could curb borrowers’ appetite.
  • Hyperscaler bond issuance is nearing $300 billion this year and is expected to rise more slowly in 2027, with AI-related capex forecast to top $1.3 trillion.
  • China is likely to remain a source of issuance growth as falling government bond yields lower borrowing costs.
  • Demand for sovereign and corporate debt remains robust, and corporate bond spreads have narrowed.

Growth in global bond issuance is set to slow sharply next year, with S&P Global Ratings forecasting a 2.7% increase in 2027, down from an estimated 12.2% this year and the weakest pace in five years, according to reports of its latest outlook published Tuesday.

The slowdown comes off a very high base. S&P expects total global issuance to reach around $11.7 trillion in 2026, so even modest growth next year would keep volumes at very large levels. The forecast points to a loss of momentum rather than a retreat by borrowers from debt markets.

Two factors could hold issuers back, according to S&P. Interest rates remain elevated, raising the cost of new borrowing and of refinancing existing debt, and uncertainty linked to the Middle East war could make some borrowers more cautious about timing. Many issuers have limited room to wait, however, with maturing corporate debt needing to be refinanced and governments continuing to borrow to cover defence spending and the costs of ageing populations.

Artificial intelligence remains one of the main sources of supply. Bond issuance by hyperscalers, the large cloud and data centre operators financing AI infrastructure, is approaching $300 billion this year, and S&P expects it to rise again in 2027, though at a slower pace. AI-related capital expenditure is forecast to exceed $1.3 trillion next year, which suggests the largest technology companies will keep returning to debt markets to fund it.

China is expected to remain a source of growth. Falling Chinese government bond yields have lowered borrowing costs for local issuers, and continued growth in issuance there could gradually lift China’s weight in major bond benchmarks. That would increase the exposure of index-tracking funds to Chinese interest rate moves and to currency hedging decisions.

Demand has so far kept pace with supply. S&P said appetite for sovereign and corporate debt remains robust, and corporate bond spreads, the extra yield investors demand over government debt, have narrowed, indicating that investors have absorbed this year’s heavy issuance without requiring much additional compensation.

The 2027 outlook therefore hinges less on investor demand than on the cost of borrowing. If rates stay high and geopolitical uncertainty persists, issuance growth could stay subdued beyond next year. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.description:
The major US stock indices closed higher, but the gains were far from evenly distributed. AI and chip-related shares continued to outperform, helping the Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 rise more than 1%. The Russell 2000 also joined the rally, while the Dow industrial average finished with a modest 16-point gain.

Within the Magnificent 7, Tesla led the way with a 4.04% advance, followed by Amazon. However, Microsoft and Meta moved lower. Meta’s decline also carried a bearish technical development as the price moved below both its 100-day and 200-day moving averages and finished near the session low.

AI and chip shares extend their leadership

The strongest gains on the supplied watchlist stretched across AI infrastructure, semiconductors, connectivity, storage and power-related shares. This was more than a rally in the largest technology names. Several companies further down the market-cap ladder delivered gains well above those of the broader indices.

Some of the standout performers have been under pressure lately but snapped back higher today.  Included:

  • AMD: +5.45% to $560.26.

The size of those advances shows where buyers were most aggressive. Nvidia participated as well, but its 0.90% gain was relatively modest compared with the larger moves elsewhere in the group.  

Tesla and Amazon lead the Mag 7

Tesla rose 4.04% to $407.46, comfortably leading the Magnificent 7. Amazon followed with a 1.61% gain to $253.10 ahead of Thursday’s earnings release.

Alphabet also advanced ahead of its report tomorrow, while Microsoft slipped modestly. The complete scoreboard for the Mag7 stocks showed:

  • Tesla: +4.04% to $407.46.

  • Amazon: +1.61% to $253.10.

  • Alphabet: +1.19% to $320.58.

  • Apple: +0.93% to $347.10.

  • Nvidia: +0.90% to $217.94.

  • Microsoft: −0.22% to $531.44.

  • Meta: −1.64% to $620.19.

Five of the seven finished higher, but the divergence remains important. Buyers continued to favor selected technology shares, while others struggled even with the Nasdaq moving solidly higher.

Meta sellers take more control

Meta was the weakest of the seven, falling $10.37 and closing near its low for the day. More importantly from a technical perspective, the price moved below both its 100-day and 200-day moving averages.

That shifts the burden to the buyers. To improve the technical picture, they need to push the price back above those moving averages and keep it there. Until that happens, the broken levels become potential resistance on a recovery.

A quick recovery would raise the possibility of a failed break. Continued trading below both moving averages would reinforce the bearish bias. Closing near the low adds to the concern, as buyers were unable to produce a meaningful recovery by the finish.

The trading lesson: Follow the individual stock’s clues

A rising Nasdaq can provide a supportive backdrop, but each stock still needs to confirm its own bullish bias. Meta’s weakness on a strong day for technology is a useful reminder.

Moving averages help traders define that distinction. Once the price breaks below an important moving average, the next question is whether it can recover and stay above it. That gives traders a practical barometer for judging control and defining risk.

For Meta, the sellers have made their play. The buyers now need to respond.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: ICYMI: Fitch sees Fed hiking to 4.25% in December, says US credit outlook still benign
item.description:
Fitch’s December call fits the view that the Fed is still on a hiking path, which supports front-end Treasury yields and the US dollar and argues against any near-term easing. The more telling signal for credit is the split it describes: investment-grade spreads near multi-year lows while CCC yields have blown out. Heavy hyperscaler issuance on top of Treasury supply raises the risk that new deals need bigger concessions even where credit quality holds up. For equities, putting a recession scenario next to AI capex keeps the spotlight on any sign that hyperscalers are scaling back spending plans.

---

I spotted the headlines from Fitch overngiht and just bringing it to investingLive now. Fitch trails behind S&P and Moody's but I doubt their analysis and conclusions would be too much different. 

----

Fitch still calls US credit benign overall, but its December Fed hike call, record private credit defaults and an AI-driven recession scenario show the pressure building on the weakest borrowers.

Summary:

  • Fitch expects the US credit outlook to stay broadly benign, though higher-for-longer rates and AI funding needs will test interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers.
  • It raised its US GDP forecasts for 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 point to 2.1% each, and expects the Fed to hike to 4.25% in December and hold through 2027.
  • US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months, and corporate bond issuance rose around 25%, driven partly by hyperscaler AI borrowing.
  • Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while CCC yields have widened by about 480 basis points this year.
  • Fitch calls AI both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. Its adverse AI equity-correction scenario would mean a US recession, with GDP falling 0.6% in 2027.
  • Fitch’s private credit default rate hit a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and leveraged loan defaults are expected near the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end range.

Fitch Ratings expects the US credit outlook to remain broadly benign, even as higher-for-longer interest rates and rising AI-related funding needs put interest-sensitive and lower-rated borrowers under pressure, according to a Fitch Wire commentary published Tuesday alongside its fourth-quarter US credit brief.

The ratings agency has lifted its US growth forecasts for both 2026 and 2027 by 0.2 percentage point to 2.1%, pointing to resilient consumer spending and AI-driven private investment. Fixed investment is forecast to grow 4.8% this year and 4.6% next year. On policy, Fitch expects the Federal Reserve to raise its policy rate to 4.25% in December and keep it there through 2027, which it says will sustain pressure on borrowers who need to refinance at higher costs.

Funding conditions are also being shaped by heavy Treasury supply and increased borrowing by hyperscalers, the large cloud and data centre operators, to pay for AI capital spending. Fitch said US fixed-income issuance rose around 10% year on year in the first nine months of 2026, while corporate bond issuance climbed around 25%. The picture across the credit spectrum is uneven. Investment-grade spreads remain near multi-year lows, while yields on CCC-rated debt, the lowest rung of high yield, have widened by about 480 basis points since the start of the year.

Fitch described AI investment as both the main growth driver and a key downside risk. IT-related private investment grew around 18% year on year in the second quarter, but the agency warned that intensifying competition and cheaper open-weight models could weaken the pricing power of AI service providers and prompt a rethink of hyperscaler capex plans over the next one to three years. Under Fitch’s adverse AI equity-correction scenario, the US would fall into recession, with GDP contracting 0.6% in 2027. Its sector-level AI stress test found broad resilience, with material risks concentrated in services, data centres, and telecommunications, media and technology.

Higher rates are weighing most heavily on housing-related sectors and lower-rated borrowers. Fitch’s US private credit default rate reached a record 6.3% in the 12 months to September, and the agency expects leveraged loan defaults to rise toward the low end of its 4.5% to 5.0% year-end forecast range.

The commentary leaves the Fed’s December decision and the durability of AI spending as the two variables most likely to determine whether a benign outlook for credit overall holds up for its weakest borrowers. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: AUDUSD trades up and down in a 35 pip trading range over the last 3 days. Look for a break?
item.description:
The AUDUSD has spent the last three trading days moving up and down inside a narrow range, with a low near 0.7005 and a high at 0.70397. That is only about 35 pips from bottom to top. There has been plenty of movement within that range, but limited progress for either the buyers or the sellers.

In the video above, I take a look at the technical levels defining that battle and explain why traders should be preparing for a potential break and run.

The moving averages tell the story of indecision

Inside the range sit two key technical levels: the 100-hour moving average near 0.7023 and the 100-day moving average at 0.70317.

The price has been trading above and below those moving averages. A move above has not generated enough buying momentum to get away. A move below has not led to a sustained push lower either. That back-and-forth price action tells us that neither side has been able to take firm control.

Moving averages can be useful barometers for the trading bias. However, when the price repeatedly crosses them in a narrow range, traders need to recognize what the market is saying: the directional conviction is limited, and the market is waiting for a catalyst.

That catalyst could come from economic data, central bank commentary, or a broader shift in the USD or risk sentiment. The technical chart does not tell us which headline will do it. It does give us levels to judge whether the reaction is changing the picture.

What would give the buyers more control?

For the buyers, getting above the 100-hour moving average near 0.7023 is a start. Moving above the 100-day moving average at 0.70317 would add to the bullish tilt.

However, the buyers also need to get above—and stay above—the range high at 0.70397. That would take the price outside the ceiling that has limited the upside over the last three days.

A sustained break would open the door toward the 200-day moving average at 0.70535, followed by the 50% retracement at 0.70654.

Those become the next hurdles. If the price breaks higher but quickly falls back below the range high and the moving averages, the failed break would raise questions about the buyers’ conviction.

What would give the sellers more control?

On the downside, a move below the moving averages would shift the focus back toward the range low near 0.7005.

A break below that floor would put the 200-hour moving average near 0.69979 into play, followed by the swing area around 0.6990.

The sellers would need to get through those levels to build on the break. If the price falls below the range and then quickly moves back inside it, the downside attempt would also lose credibility.

Anticipate the opportunity. Let the price confirm it.

A narrow range does not guarantee that a big move is coming immediately. The range can remain narrow, and an initial break can fail.

However, the best traders anticipate what might happen next. They recognize the compression, identify the levels that matter, and prepare a game plan for either direction.

For the AUDUSD, the question is whether the next push outside 0.7005–0.70397 can attract enough follow-through to get the market moving.

The opportunity comes from a break that can stay broken. Until then, the buyers and sellers remain locked in the same narrow battle.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Macro takeaways from earnings: Travel, package delivery and home appliances in focus
item.description:
The US economy is sending some wildly contradictory signals, but four earnings calls this today help to make sense of what's happening beneath the surface.

Whirlpool is struggling with weak consumer demand and says Americans are putting off appliance purchases. Royal Caribbean is seeing record cruise bookings at higher prices. Hilton says business travel is booming as the AI and infrastructure investment cycle accelerates, while UPS is seeing explosive growth in high-tech shipments but a mixed picture elsewhere.

At first glance, those are four very different stories. Taken together, they paint a picture of an economy that's still growing, but increasingly divided between asset owners and everyone else, with a powerful capital spending boom providing an additional engine of growth.

Perhaps the most revealing comment came from UPS CEO Carol Tomé:

"It's a bit of a K curve for sure. If you have assets, you're spending. If you don't, you're stretched."

That might be the best summary of the US consumer right now.

The consumer is still spending, but not on everything

Whirlpool expects North American appliance industry demand to decline around 5% this year, with the company describing persistent weakness in discretionary purchases.

CEO Marc Bitzer said consumers are increasingly focused on replacing appliances only when they have to, and even some replacement decisions are being delayed.

"We've seen in situations in the past where you had a very negative consumer confidence or elements that people even hold back some replacement decisions."

He specifically mentioned dishwashers and secondary appliances.

Even when consumers do make purchases, they're watching their budgets closely. Bitzer said customers might enter a store determined to spend no more than $600 on a washing machine. If prices rise, they don't necessarily abandon the purchase, but they move down to a cheaper model.

That's a particularly interesting inflation dynamic. Companies can successfully raise prices without necessarily seeing a collapse in unit demand, but the consumer absorbs the increase by sacrificing quality or features.

Worse yet, the company said it's raising prices 7% starting December 3 compounding a 9% hike from January. 

"We will take the lead, and that's what we're doing because it reflects real cost, it reflects real material costs and real tariff costs," Bitzer said.

Royal Caribbean is also raising prices but it's demand led.

The cruise operator reported that booking volumes since its previous earnings call increased by a mid-teens percentage year-over-year, while bookings for 2027 sailings were up by a high-teens percentage.

The company has more bookings at record rates, and spending onboard ships has been stronger than management expected.

CEO Jason Liberty put it plainly:

"Customers are willing to pay us more in the future and today than they did yesterday."

There is no sign of a consumer retrenchment in those numbers.

Of course, these aren't necessarily the same consumers. Royal Caribbean is benefiting from households with the disposable income to take vacations, while Whirlpool is exposed to a much broader consumer base, including people who are feeling the squeeze from higher living costs.

UPS sees that divide clearly, but its overall assessment of the consumer remains constructive. The company cited industry projections for roughly 9% growth in holiday online retail sales and expects a normal seasonal surge in package volumes.

The AI boom is showing up in places you might not expect

Perhaps the most encouraging economic signal came from Hilton and UPS.

There has been plenty of debate about whether the enormous sums being spent on artificial intelligence are creating a broader economic benefit or simply circulating among a handful of technology giants.

These earnings calls provide tangible evidence of the spillover effects.

Hilton reported that global business transient revenue per available room rose 8.3% in the third quarter, with US manufacturing, technology and workforce lodging all growing more than 10%.

CEO Chris Nassetta tied that strength directly to investment in data centres, energy infrastructure, manufacturing and public infrastructure.

"When people are investing, people have to run around the country and do it."

His argument is straightforward: Someone has to build the data centres, power plants, factories, bridges and highways. Those workers, engineers and managers need hotel rooms.

Nassetta said growth in nonresidential fixed investment has been running at nearly twice its 20-year historical average for six to seven quarters.

That investment is also helping the middle of the hotel market recover, with business travel increasingly approaching pre-pandemic levels.

UPS provided another striking confirmation.

Its US high-tech small-package business grew 30% year-over-year in the third quarter.

Tomé emphasized that the increase wasn't coming from a tiny starting point:

"Not on a small base, but 30% year-on-year."

UPS estimates that data centres alone represent a $15 billion logistics opportunity.

So there are two very different companies reporting the same underlying trend. Hilton is accommodating the people building the infrastructure, while UPS is transporting the components and equipment.

This is an important signal for the economic outlook because it suggests AI investment is supporting activity well beyond semiconductors and cloud computing.

It also helps explain why parts of the economy can remain strong even as interest-sensitive consumer spending struggles.

Small businesses may be doing better than expected

Another encouraging signal comes from small and medium-sized businesses.

UPS reported a 3.7% year-over-year increase in average daily package volume (not price) from small and medium-sized businesses, with growth across nearly all industries.

Meanwhile, Hilton said its business travel recovery is being supported by both large companies and smaller businesses.

These numbers aren't perfect indicators of overall small-business health. UPS is deliberately shifting toward higher-value customers, while Hilton benefits from businesses engaged in capital projects.

Still, it's notable that both companies are reporting strength in these segments.

Inflation is not finished

The other important takeaway is that pricing pressures remain substantial.

Whirlpool said US steel prices have risen nearly 50% over the past year, despite falling iron ore prices and much lower international steel prices.

Bitzer described the divergence as disconnected from underlying fundamentals. It's ironic that a company that's directly benefitting from tariffs on foreign appliances is also complaining about higher prices from steel tariffs.

The company is also dealing with rising resin, fuel, transportation and tariff costs. Those pressures are being passed through to consumers.

UPS is seeing pricing power as well. Domestic revenue per package rose 6.1% year-over-year, although roughly half of that reflected higher fuel charges. Management expects base pricing and mix to contribute another 2-3 percentage points going forward.

At Royal Caribbean, customers are accepting higher prices and spending more once they're onboard.

There is a difference between cost-driven price increases at Whirlpool and demand-driven pricing at Royal Caribbean, but the result is a reminder that disinflation won't necessarily proceed smoothly across the economy.

In particular, the combination of tariffs, elevated domestic steel costs and higher energy prices threatens to keep pressure on goods prices even in categories where demand is weak.

What it means for the Fed and markets

The overall picture is of an economy that's much harder to characterize than the headline data suggest.

There is clear weakness in interest-sensitive consumer spending, particularly durable goods. Some consumers are delaying purchases and trading down as higher prices strain household budgets.

But there is also unmistakable strength in travel, business investment and some parts of the services economy.

And the AI infrastructure buildout is increasingly providing a bridge between the technology sector and the broader economy.

For the Federal Reserve, that's a complicated combination.

Weakness in durable goods and stretched households argues for caution about the growth outlook, but resilient services spending, strong investment demand and another round of cost-driven price increases make it difficult to declare victory over inflation.

The comments from UPS, Hilton, Royal Caribbean and Whirlpool don't point to an economy on the verge of collapse. Nor do they describe one where everyone is prospering.

Instead, they point to an economy increasingly supported by two forces: spending from households with assets and an extraordinary investment cycle in technology and infrastructure.

The question for 2027 is whether those forces will be enough to lift the rest of the economy, or whether the gap between the winners and losers continues to widen.

item.title: Flávio Bolsonaro reportedly flees Brazil for the US after election loss
item.description:
Flávio Bolsonaro is reportedly en route to the United States, according to allies cited by Folha de S.Paulo. That comes just two days after he lost the presidential runoff to Lula, and after the Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports amid criminal investigations. Brazilian authorities then cancelled his Brazilian passport.

Allies say he went out through Argentina. Nothing about the route or his current location has been confirmed, so treat this with some caution until there’s an official word.

If it’s accurate, this goes well beyond a losing candidate leaving the country. A presidential runner-up under investigation, travelling without a valid passport, would be landing in a country whose president openly backed him. The family already has a foothold there. His brother Eduardo told Reuters he has received permanent US residency, and has lived in the US since February 2025. Flávio met Trump in the Oval Office back in May. Brasília also denied visas to two US diplomats this summer after spotting a possible link between Flávio’s attacks on the voting machines and the Trump administration.

So the setup is a likely extradition fight, Washington possibly treating him as a political exile, and a US-Brazil relationship that was already strained heading toward an ugly patch right as Lula starts a new term. It's almost certain that Trump would grant him asylum but it might be more tricky in a subsequent administration. It could also hinge on the charges, which are money laundering and illegal transfers abroad.

For markets, I don’t see this as a BRL story yet. The election is already enough for the currency to deal with and the challenger leaving the country is about as conclusive an ending as you can get. It does raise questions about the future of any Bolsonaro movement, but effectively ends it. His father Jair remains under house arrest.

The risk is on the bilateral side. If this escalates into tariff threats, sanctions on Brazilian officials or a trade spat, that’s the channel that would hit Brazilian assets. Watch for any comment from the White House or the State Department.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: European stocks mostly rise, but the FTSE lags as French yields climb
item.description:
As London/European traders head home, the major continental indices are closing higher, with Italy and Germany leading the gains. The UK FTSE 100 is the exception, moving lower as weakness in HSBC weighs on sentiment. Meanwhile, the French bond market continues to flash caution, with yields rising despite the recovery in French equities.

Italy and Germany lead. HSBC weighs on the FTSE

Germany’s DAX gained 195.79 points, or 0.77%, to 25,606.64, while France’s CAC 40 rose 39.82 points, or 0.51%, to 7,887.15. Spain’s Ibex advanced 127.30 points, or 0.67%, to 19,160.60, and Italy’s FTSE MIB led the group with a 441.14-point gain, or 0.90%, to 49,627.94. In contrast, the UK FTSE 100 fell 80.77 points, or 0.75%, to 10,686.55.

HSBC was a drag after disappointing revenue sent its shares down nearly 7% earlier in the session. Elsewhere, Novartis raised its earnings outlook, while BE Semiconductor Industries benefited from news that Applied Materials increased its stake to 20%. Investors are also preparing for the Fed decision Wednesday and the ECB decision Thursday. www.reuters.com

French confidence sinks as the bond spread widens

France remains a concern. Consumer confidence fell five points to 80, its lowest reading since June 2013, as protests against government economic policies continued. That leaves the recovery in French stocks taking place against a difficult domestic backdrop. www.aol.com

The bond market reflects that unease. France’s benchmark 10-year yield rose 2.4 basis points to 4.927%, while Germany’s fell 0.9 basis point to 3.361%. That puts the French premium over Germany at 156.6 basis points, widening another 3.3 basis points on the day. Equity buyers are making a play, but the widening spread suggests investors still want additional compensation to hold French debt.

Elsewhere, Italy’s 10-year yield increased 1.4 basis points to 4.514%, Spain’s slipped 0.3 basis point to 4.005%, and the UK yield was little changed at 5.353%, up 0.1 basis point.

US orders and confidence improve, but consumers remain cautious

In the US, the economic releases painted a mixed picture, with manufacturing orders and consumer confidence improving while housing activity remained softer.

September durable goods orders rose 1.8%, following a 0.1% increase in August. Transportation led the advance with a 4.6% gain, but orders excluding transportation also increased 0.5%. The underlying increase suggests the improvement extended beyond the volatile transportation category, although that category supplied most of the headline gain. www.census.gov

Consumer confidence also rebounded. The Conference Board index increased to 91.7 from an upwardly revised 84.2, with improvements in both current conditions and expectations. However, the details were more restrained: consumers planned less spending on services and durable goods, while inflation expectations remained elevated at 5.8%. Confidence improved, but households are still watching their purchasing power. www.conference-board.org

Housing sales soften while prices continue higher

September new home sales slipped 0.6% to a 676,000 annualized pace, from 680,000 in August, and were 5.3% below a year earlier. Inventory declined to 476,000 homes, but supply remained elevated at 8.4 months. Builders have fewer homes available than a month ago, but the sales pace is still leaving buyers with considerable choice.

Meanwhile, the FHFA reported that home prices increased 0.3% in August and 2.4% year over year. July’s monthly gain was revised down to 0.2% from 0.3%. Prices are still moving higher nationally, adding to the affordability challenge even as sales remain subdued.

US 10-year yield presses against the 5% barometer

US Treasury yields were higher across the curve in the supplied snapshot, with the larger increases at the short end. The 2-year yield rose 2.38 basis points to 4.7348%, the 5-year increased 1.65 basis points to 4.8405%, and the 10-year edged up 0.86 basis point to 4.9946%. The 30-year yield rose 0.72 basis point to 5.3082%.

That leaves the 10-year just below the 5.00% barometer as traders await the Fed. A sustained move above that level would keep borrowing costs and equity valuations firmly in focus.

Dollar gains across the major currencies

The dollar was also firmer across the major currencies. EURUSD fell 0.30% to 1.1139, while GBPUSD declined 0.24% to 1.3307. USDJPY rose 0.23% to 157.86, USDCHF advanced 0.19% to 0.8287, and USDCAD increased 0.26% to 1.4047.

The AUDUSD and NZDUSD were also lower, trading at 0.7029 and 0.5685, respectively. The gains across the board point to broad dollar demand heading into the Fed decision.

Oil tests $100 while gold finds buyers

In commodities, crude oil moved lower while metals found buyers. The December crude contract fell $1.49, or 1.46%, to $100.27. The $100 level is the nearby psychological barometer. Staying below that level would add to the pullback; holding above it would leave sellers with more work to do.

Gold gained despite the firmer dollar and higher Treasury yields. Spot gold rose $43.51, or 1.08%, to $4,060.70, while silver advanced 0.88% to $54.41 and copper climbed 1.68% to $6.6520. Bitcoin also edged higher, gaining 0.49% to $80,400, keeping the price close to the familiar $80,000 pivot.

Fed and technology earnings are the next tests

Attention now turns to the central banks and the next round of technology earnings. Microsoft and Alphabet report Wednesday, followed by Amazon Thursday, putting the returns from heavy AI spending back under scrutiny. For traders, the question is whether the improving equity tone can build momentum with US yields still pressing against 5%

item.title: Why spreads matter more than you think, Elev8 broker explains
item.description:
The spread, the difference between the bid (selling price) and ask (buying price)—can become a substantial expense when trades are frequent. According to the World Gold Council, average spot-market spreads were 0.02% for gold (XAUUSD) and 0.09% for silver (XAGUSD) between February 2025 and February 2026. It means your choice of instrument can multiply your spread costs: for the same trade value, spreads on silver were 4.5 times higher than on gold. 

Spreads are also essential for traders who use Contracts for Difference (CFD) as their main instrument. Elev8, a global CFD broker, explains how spreads work, how repeated transactions can turn small price differences into measurable trading costs, and why those costs matter in financial markets.

What costs does a trader pay on every trade?

Trading costs fall into four main categories: spreads, commissions, swaps, and taxes. Slippage is another potential cost factor, but because it is unpredictable and irregular, it will not be covered in this article. The spread is built into the buying and selling prices, while the other costs depend on the account, holding period, and applicable tax rules. A spread creates a cost even when a trade has no separate commission.

 

What are spreads in trading?

The spread is the difference between the ask (the price you buy at) and the bid (the price you sell at). Unlike a separate commission, the spread is built into the quoted prices. When a trader opens a position, the platform values an immediate exit at the opposite side of the quote, which explains why a new position immediately shows a small unrealised loss.

Spread costs accumulate with every completed trade, reducing profits or adding to losses. The effect is particularly relevant to day trading (opening and closing positions within the same trading day) and scalping (making frequent, short-duration trades targeting small price movements). The smaller the targeted price movement, the greater the share that the spread can absorb. For example, a 30-pip spread absorbs 15% of a targeted 200-pip move, 30% of a 100-pip move, and 60% of a 50-pip move, before other costs. 

How much can a small difference in the XAUUSD spread cost an active trader?

XAUUSD spreads vary across brokers and trading sessions. During liquid hours, particularly the London–New York overlap, spreads may fall within a range of 0.15–0.30. During quieter parts of the Asian session, at rollover (when positions are carried into the next trading day), or around major news releases, spreads can widen substantially—sometimes severalfold.

For day traders and scalpers, spread changes directly affect the economics of a trade. Assuming the spread on XAUUSD is 30 pips ($0.30), if a trader is aiming for a tight $0.50 take-profit target, over half of their gross potential profit ($0.60 out of $1.00) is instantly consumed by the spread alone—before factoring in swaps, commissions, or slippage. It clearly demonstrates why tight spreads are critical for intraday strategies. 

'Gold's liquidity and price volatility can make XAUUSD attractive to active traders, but neither guarantees that price movements will outweigh spread costs. Gold spreads respond to changes in available liquidity: during sharp moves triggered by economic news or geopolitical events, spreads can widen, making entry and exit more expensive precisely when traders want to act', notes Kar Yong Ang, a financial market analyst at Elev8.

'For traders targeting gold’s short-term fluctuations, a wider XAUUSD spread increases the price movement needed to break even. If the movement captured is smaller than the spread, the trade loses money even when the trader correctly anticipates the market’s direction', he adds.

How do spreads affect different trading styles?

Spread costs matter most when trades are frequent and targeted price movements are small. Holding positions for longer generally reduces the spread’s relative impact, although position size and the number of entries and exits still matter.

Here's a more detailed breakdown of how spreads affect different trading styles.

  • Day trading. Repeated transactions accumulate spread costs throughout the day. A lower spread reduces the price movement needed to cover trading expenses.
  • Scalping. The spread can absorb a substantial share—or all—of the targeted movement. Keeping spread costs low is particularly important to the strategy's viability.
  • Swing trading (holding positions for days or weeks). Larger targeted movements generally make the spread a smaller proportion of potential gains. Frequent re-entry or opening and closing positions in stages increases accumulated costs.
  • Long-term positions. The spread generally matters less relative to the overall price movement. Where applicable, swaps (overnight financing charges or credits) can have a greater cumulative impact, but the spread still affects entry and exit costs.

This is a middling reading but it's rarely a market mover. Prices paid appear to have stabilized.

For background, the Richmond Fed’s Fifth District Survey of Manufacturing Activity is a monthly gauge of factory conditions across Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, the District of Columbia and most of West Virginia. It’s released at 10 am ET, usually on the fourth Tuesday of the month, alongside the bank’s companion survey of service sector activity.

The headline is a composite manufacturing index, a weighted average of three components: new orders, shipments and employment. Like the other regional Fed surveys, each measure is a diffusion index calculated as the percentage of firms reporting an increase minus the percentage reporting a decrease, so zero marks the line between expansion and contraction.

Beyond the composite, the survey tracks backlogs of orders, capacity utilization, vendor lead times, wages and local business conditions, each with a matching expectations index for six months ahead. Its price data are presented differently from most regional surveys. Rather than a diffusion index, firms report the annualized growth rate of prices paid and prices received, giving a direct read on how fast costs and selling prices are rising, along with expectations for the next 12 months.

The district’s manufacturing base leans toward furniture, textiles, chemicals, food processing and transportation equipment, which makes it a useful window on parts of the industrial economy that don’t show up as clearly in Texas or New York.

The Richmond survey is one of the smaller regional reports and rarely moves markets on its own. Its value is in rounding out the regional picture alongside the Empire State, Philadelphia, Kansas City and Dallas surveys ahead of the national ISM manufacturing index.

item.title: October US consumer confidence 91.7 vs 81.0 expected
item.description:
• Prior was 81.9 (revised to 84.2)
  • Present situation 120.4 vs 111.8 prior
  • Expectations 72.6 vs 65.7 prior

This is a nice jump but it comes after the worst reading since 2014 so it's still at extremely depressed levels. In any case, I struggle to see the value of this indicator as anything but a political barometer. That's valuable ahead of the midterms but it doesn't tell us much about spending. Royal Caribbean cruise lines and Hilton both reported earnings today and highlighted strong -- if not strengthening demand. That skews affluent but that's the economy right now.

Hilton CEO Christopher Nassetta said the company was seeing:

"momentum across our system, which we expect to continue for the remainder of the year and into 2027."

RCL CEO Jason Liberty said:

"2027 bookings are pacing ahead of historical levels at higher rates." and highlighted "continued strong consumer demand for our vacation experiences".

In the release  Fergus McCormick, Senior Economist, Global Indicators, The Conference Board said:

“Consumer confidence advanced in October, driven primarily by improved perceptions of current and expected business conditions... The recovery was in line with retail gasoline prices easing from September to October. Yet, despite the increase in October, consumer confidence remained on the long-term downward trend that’s persisted over the past few years. Consumers planned less spending on services and durable goods over the next six months. This likely reflected higher price levels and persistent inflation, which eroded consumers’ purchasing power.”

For background, the Conference Board’s Consumer Confidence Index is one of the two major monthly gauges of US household sentiment, alongside the University of Michigan survey. It’s released at 10 am ET on the last Tuesday of the month and is indexed to 100 in 1985.

The headline index is built from questions on current business and labor market conditions and on expectations for the next six months. It splits into two sub-indexes. The Present Situation Index captures views on business conditions and job availability now. The Expectations Index reflects views on business conditions, employment and income six months out. The Conference Board has flagged readings of the Expectations Index below 80 as a historical signal of recession ahead.

The survey leans more heavily on the job market than the Michigan survey does, which makes its labor questions some of the most watched in the report. Economists track the labor differential, the share of respondents saying jobs are “plentiful” minus those saying jobs are “hard to get.” It closely tracks the unemployment rate and can give an early hint of a softening job market before it shows up in payrolls.

The report also includes 12-month inflation expectations, plans to buy homes, cars and major appliances, and views on stock prices and interest rates. Write-in responses offer a sense of what’s on consumers’ minds, such as prices, tariffs, politics or jobs.

Like other sentiment surveys, consumer confidence doesn’t always line up with actual spending, and markets tend to react only to large surprises.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

  • Average sales price: $472,800 vs $470,800 in August. Up 0.4% MoM; down 6.7% YoY.

Regional breakdown: Northeast and West gains offset by declines elsewhere

September new home sales were mixed across the regions, with gains in the Northeast and West offset by declines in the larger South market and the Midwest. All sales figures below are seasonally adjusted annual rates.

September compared with August:

  • Northeast: 32,000 vs 25,000. Up 28.0% MoM.

  • Midwest: 89,000 vs 96,000. Down 7.3% MoM.

  • South: 413,000 vs 442,000. Down 6.6% MoM.

  • West: 142,000 vs 117,000. Up 21.4% MoM.

Compared with September 2025:

  • Northeast: 32,000 vs 29,000. Up 10.3% YoY.

  • Midwest: 89,000 vs 97,000. Down 8.2% YoY.

  • South: 413,000 vs 416,000. Down 0.7% YoY.

  • West: 142,000 vs 172,000. Down 17.4% YoY.

The South was the biggest drag on the monthly result, with its annualized sales pace falling by 29,000. That more than offset the 25,000 increase in the West, while the Northeast’s gain matched the Midwest’s decline.

The annual comparison tells a different story. The West accounted for 30,000 of the 38,000 decline in the national sales pace from a year earlier. September’s strong monthly rebound in that region therefore represents a partial recovery, with sales still well below last September.

One caution: regional estimates are volatile.

Overall....

US new home sales edged lower in September, with the Census Bureau and Department of Housing and Urban Development reporting a seasonally adjusted annual sales pace of 676,000, down from 680,000 in August. Sales were 5.3% below their year-earlier level.

Inventory also declined, leaving 476,000 homes available for sale. That brought supply down slightly to 8.4 months, but it remained above the 8.2 months recorded a year earlier. Builders have fewer homes on the market than last September, but the slower sales pace means those homes represent a larger supply relative to demand.

The median price rebounded 3.9% on the month to $400,400, although both median and average prices remained below year-earlier levels. The monthly price bounce needs some perspective: changes in the mix of homes sold can move these figures without indicating an equivalent change in underlying home values.

Quick analysis: The report points to subdued demand, with ample supply relative to the sales pace. That could keep builders competing through pricing and incentives and may limit their appetite to accelerate construction. The monthly price rebound is an offset, but it does not establish renewed pricing strength.

At the margin, softer housing activity could support lower Treasury yields and weigh on the dollar. However, the reported monthly and annual sales declines fall within the release’s margins of error, limiting the strength of the signal from this report alone.

What this report measures: New home sales track sales of newly built single-family houses, generally when a contract is signed or a deposit is accepted. The headline is seasonally adjusted and annualized—it shows the yearly pace implied by that month’s activity, rather than the number actually sold during the month. Traders monitor the report for clues about housing demand, construction activity and the economy’s sensitivity to interest rates.

item.title: Bitcoin trades in a narrow range above and below $80,000. What would get the digital currency out of its rut?
item.description:
Bitcoin has been moving lower since the September and October highs formed a ceiling near $87,374. The repeated failures near that level gave sellers a clearly defined area to lean against. Buyers had their opportunities to extend the upside, but they could not sustain a break. The price has since worked its way lower.

However, the sellers have also run into a limit.

The $80,000 area continues to attract buying interest, slowing the decline and leaving the digital currency trading in a narrow range above and below that key level. Sellers have the short-term technical advantage, but they still need to prove they can break the floor and stay below it.

In the video above, I take a closer look at the technical levels defining the battle, what would open the door for more downside, and what buyers need to do to regain control.

The September and October highs defined the ceiling

The repeated highs near $86,969 to $87,374 established an important ceiling. When multiple rallies stall in the same area, traders take notice. Sellers gain a level against which to define risk, while buyers know what needs to be broken to extend the trend higher.

Since the last failure at that ceiling, the price has moved lower and is now trading below both its 100-hour moving average at $80,408 and its 200-hour moving average at $81,403.

That keeps the short-term bias tilted toward the sellers. However, the support below has prevented them from turning that advantage into a more sustained move lower.

The $80,000 area remains the downside barometer

The chart shows a well-tested swing area around $79,580 to $80,000. That area has acted as both support and resistance, making it a key barometer for traders.

The number of tests matters. Buyers continue to defend the area, but each return also puts that support under pressure.

For sellers, a brief dip below $80,000 is only a start. They need to push below the swing area and sustain the break. A move through $79,146 (the low from the weekend trade) would add to the downside momentum and give traders another reason to look toward the next major support cluster.

That cluster includes:

  • $76,052: The 38.2% retracement of the advance from the July low.

  • $75,754: The 100-day moving average.

  • $74,925: The lower swing support level.

Together, those levels define a broader support zone between $74,925 and $76,052. With a retracement, a major daily moving average, and prior swing support converging, that area would become an important test if the current floor gives way.

What would give buyers more control?

The first step is to get back above the 100-hour moving average at $80,408 and stay above it. That would ease some of the immediate downside pressure.

The more meaningful step would be a sustained move above the 200-hour moving average at $81,403. Clearing both moving averages would give buyers more control and provide a stronger technical foundation for a recovery toward $83,062, followed by $84,178.

Until then, holding support helps the buyers keep a foothold, but they need to reclaim resistance to shift the bias.

Bitcoin has a floor around $80,000 and moving-average resistance overhead. A sustained break below the floor would strengthen the sellers’ hand. A move back above both hourly moving averages would give buyers their opportunity to take back control.

item.title: US August Case-Shiller 20-city house price index +2.7% y/y vs +2.6% expected
item.description:
• Prior was +2.5% y/y
  • 20-city house price index +0.3% m/m vs +0.3% expected

Mortgage rates at 7.5% aren't doing any favors for the housing market.

For background, the S&P Case-Shiller Home Price Indices are the best-known measure of US house prices. They’re published on the last Tuesday of each month at 9 am ET and carry a roughly two-month lag, so a release in late October covers August.

The indexes use a repeat-sales method, tracking price changes on the same single-family homes as they sell over time. Because they compare a property with itself, they avoid the distortions that come from changes in the mix of homes being sold, a weakness of simple median price measures. Each monthly reading is a three-month moving average, which smooths the data but adds to the lag.

The headline figure is usually the year-over-year change in the 20-city composite index. S&P also publishes a 10-city composite and a national index, along with results for each of the 20 metro areas, which often show sharp regional divergence. Markets focus on the unadjusted annual changes, though seasonally adjusted monthly figures are available.

The Federal Housing Finance Agency releases its own house price index at the same time. It covers homes financed with conforming mortgages backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac and tends to tell a similar story.

The long lag means Case-Shiller rarely moves markets, and by the time it’s released, mortgage rates and housing activity may already have shifted. Its value is in tracking the broad trend in home values, which matters for household wealth, consumer spending and the health of the housing sector. Home prices don’t feed directly into CPI, where shelter costs are measured through rents, but sustained price gains can affect rents and affordability over time.

item.title: Another Apple launch is off to a bad start
item.description:
It’s starting to feel like Apple’s tradition: every big launch comes with a problem. The iPhone 4 had signal issues when held a certain way, the iPhone 6 Plus was bending in people’s pockets, and the iPhone 15 Pro was getting unusually hot until an iOS update helped fix it.

Now it’s the iPhone Duo’s turn. Just hours after sales kicked off, reports of screens cracking along the fold started coming in, though Apple says only a small number of devices are affected and has advised customers to contact AppleCare for a replacement.

Apple shares slipped around 1% on the news, not a huge move, but could this turn into a bigger problem?

In similar cases, Apple shares have typically dipped 3–5% over a few days, without driving customers away. Most users have stayed loyal, waiting for fixes rather than switching brands, while Wall Street has quickly moved on, knowing Apple has plenty of cash to cover repairs and legal costs.

It’s also worth noting that the iPhone Duo was never expected to be a game-changer for Apple’s revenue. Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, expects Apple to sell 20 million units in fiscal 2027, accounting for roughly 7% of total iPhone sales that year.

But there’s another risk that could hit Apple: AI.

Rising financing costs, power shortages for data centers, intensifying competition between AI models, and doubts over whether massive investments will pay off have investors demanding proof that all this spending is actually driving revenue and profits.

That puts the spotlight on Big Tech earnings and how quickly AI investments translate into real revenue. Investors want to see AI spending drive sustainable revenue growth, not just larger capital budgets, and so far, few companies have convincingly demonstrated they can do so.

In particular, according to Apollo, revenue per employee in the tech sector has climbed from around $550,000 in 2022 to nearly $800,000, while the other 493 S&P 500 companies remain at roughly $550,000. Tech profit margins have also risen, while those of other companies have hovered around 10%.

The bigger question is whether AI can eventually deliver similar productivity and profit gains across the rest of the economy. If it can’t, investors may start questioning whether the massive spending is really paying off, and that could put further pressure on tech stocks, including Apple.

Keep an eye on the stock heatmap to see how Apple’s sell-off compares with broader market moves and whether weakness is spreading across major tech stocks. S&P 500 futurescan also offer an early signal of how investors are positioning ahead of the next market session, especially as Big Tech earnings and AI spending remain in focus.

  • Non-defense capital goods orders ex-air +0.5% vs +0.7% expected
  • Prior +1.6%

Durable goods orders have been chopping sideways for much of the past year and today's report is more of the same. it's a nice climb but it comes after months of stagnation.

The core number is better but this data point is rarely a market mover, even ahead of a tricky Fed decision.

On the washing machine front, Whirlpool reported earnings yesterday and they were dire, with shares falling 5% premarket to the lowest since the depths of the financial crisis. They're down 90% from the 2021 peak. The company has been in a brutal tailspin because of the deep recession in the US housing market. The company should be benefitting from tariffs but it can't seem to find traction and is now struggling under a heavy debt load.

David Tepper took a big stake last year but blew out of it and I'm sure he's glad he did because the chart is horrible.

For background, the US Census Bureau publishes its advance report on durable goods orders monthly at 8:30 am ET, roughly four weeks after the reference month ends. It covers manufacturers’ new orders, shipments, unfilled orders and inventories for durable goods, defined as products expected to last three years or more, such as machinery, vehicles, aircraft, appliances, computers and electrical equipment.

The headline figure is the monthly change in total new orders, and it’s notoriously volatile. Commercial aircraft orders, driven largely by Boeing, are lumpy and can swing the headline by several percentage points in either direction in a single month. For that reason, markets look past the headline to orders excluding transportation, which strip out aircraft and motor vehicles. Defense orders are another source of noise.

The most closely watched measure is core capital goods orders, formally nondefense capital goods excluding aircraft. It serves as a proxy for business investment plans, showing whether companies are committing to spend on equipment. Core capital goods shipments are equally important, because they feed directly into the equipment investment component of GDP, and economists often adjust their growth forecasts after the report.

The advance figures are revised about a week later in the full factory orders report, which adds nondurable goods. Revisions can be significant, particularly for the volatile categories.

The report rarely moves markets dramatically but can shift the outlook for capital spending. In recent years it has captured several cross-currents, including tariff front-running, supply chain reshoring and heavy investment in data center and power equipment tied to artificial intelligence.
